children: By Karen Sloan

With its status as the federally recognized accreditor of US law schools in jeopardy, the American Bar Association will make its case in Washington on Wednesday to continue overseeing the institutions that educate the nation’s lawyers.

The ABA’s law school oversight arm is set to appear before a US Department of Education committee after staff at the agency recommended ending its accreditor status, which the ABA has held since 1952.
The meeting comes amid an escalating conflict between President Donald Trump's administration and the ABA, the country's most-recognized attorney organization with about 150,000 dues-paying members.

Trump and the ABA have clashed over his executive orders targeting law firms and his officials’ statements criticizing judges. The ⁠US Department of Justice has barred its attorneys from speaking at or attending ABA events and curtailed the ABA’s longtime role in vetting judicial nominees. A White House spokesperson in 2025 dismissed the organization as a “snooty” group of “leftist lawyers.”

The ABA's legal education council, which currently accredits 198 US law schools, largely operates separately from the wider ABA. But it too has drawn Trump administration criticism amid a federal crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion policies in government, the private sector and academia.

Trump signed an executive order in April 2025 directing Education Secretary ⁠Linda McMahon to assess whether to suspend or terminate the ABA as the government’s official law school accreditor, citing its “unlawful" DEI requirements. Under rules the ABA repealed earlier this month, ABA-accredited schools were required to demonstrate their commitment to diversity in recruitment, admissions and student programming.

The Education Department's National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity, a bipartisan 18-member committee, is expected to make a recommendation on the ABA’s accreditor status during the Wednesday meeting, though a final decision is not expected for several months. The department reviews higher education accreditors every five years.
AGENCY SAYS ACCREDITATION ARM NOT INDEPENDENT

In an August report recommending against renewing the ABA’s accreditor status, Education Department staff concluded that the legal education council is not "separate and independent" from the larger ABA as required. The report also faulted the ABA for being too slow to revise its law school diversity rule.

Melissa Hart, chair of the ABA’s legal education council, said in a statement Tuesday that it has “consistently complied” with the Education Department’s requirements and the committee should vote to extend its accreditor recognition.
“We see no legal basis for revoking that recognition,” Hart said.
The Education Department did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday.

Revoking the ABA's accreditor status would disrupt federal student loan access for some law schools and could make it harder for law students to take the bar exam and become licensed attorneys in different states.

The committee is slated to hear from ABA representatives and Education Department staff, as well as a long list of public commenters. Registered speakers include representatives from several prominent conservative legal groups and think tanks, including the Manhattan Institute and America First Legal Foundation.

Representatives from organizations that have previously offered public comments in support of the ABA’s national network of accreditation, including the Association of American Law Schools and the National Association for Law Placement, are also scheduled to give public comment.
